opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think adapting robots to new tasks is one of the central challenges right now, and it's harder than people often expect.

The core issue is that every new task usually means starting a lot of the pipeline over. In reinforcement learning for locomotion, which is where most of my work has been, you can get a policy that walks really robustly over rough terrain. But if you want that same robot to open a door, carry a box, or climb onto a platform, you often have to redesign the reward function, rebuild the simulation environment, tune the curriculum, and then go through the whole sim-to-real transfer process again. Each of those steps takes a lot of engineering and expertise, and that doesn't scale.

Massively parallel simulation helped a lot. Being able to train thousands of robots on a single GPU turned training time from days into minutes, so iteration is much faster. But that mostly solves the compute bottleneck. The human bottleneck is still there: someone has to define what the task is, shape the reward so the robot learns the behavior you actually want instead of exploiting the simulator, and make sure the result transfers to hardware.

So I see a few directions that are promising. One is building more general low-level skills, like robust locomotion and whole-body control, that can be reused as building blocks so you aren't relearning how to balance for every new task. Another is putting higher-level reasoning on top, potentially with language or vision models, that can compose those skills and decide what to do. And then there's automating parts of the pipeline itself: generating environments, rewards, or training setups automatically rather than hand-crafting them.

The real test is whether a robot can go into a new situation and do something useful without a team of PhDs spending weeks on it. We're not there yet, but I think the pieces are starting to come together.

r001.rationale: The response calls adapting robots to new tasks a central challenge but never compares it with adapting to a new robot.

r002.rationale: The response says the real test is whether a robot can handle a new situation without a team of PhDs spending weeks on it, making the human effort required a measure of progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that adapting robots to new tasks is still one of the hardest problems we have, and it's hard in a way that's a bit different from what people expect.

When we train a legged robot to walk with reinforcement learning, we're really training it for one fairly narrow objective. We define a reward, we simulate thousands of environments in parallel, and after a few hours of training we get a controller that's incredibly robust at that one thing. The robot can walk over rough terrain, recover from pushes, climb stairs. But the moment you want it to do something slightly different, say carry a payload, open a door, or interact with an object in a way it never saw during training, you're often more or less back to square one. You need to rethink the reward, the observations, maybe the curriculum, and then retrain.

So the challenge isn't really about the policy itself being limited. It's that the whole pipeline is task specific. A lot of the engineering effort and a lot of the domain knowledge is baked into how you set up the problem. That's what makes adaptation expensive. It's not compute, compute has become cheap with GPU simulation. It's human time.

The second piece is the sim-to-real gap, which changes with the task. For locomotion we've gotten quite good at it, because we understand which physical properties matter: friction, actuator dynamics, latency, and we can randomize over them. But as soon as the task involves contact-rich manipulation, or deformable objects, or anything where perception becomes central, the simulation becomes much less trustworthy, and the tricks that worked for walking don't necessarily transfer.

What I find encouraging is that we're starting to see approaches that amortize this. Training more general policies with large task distributions, using learned models or foundation models to provide priors, or at least making the tooling flexible enough that adding a new task is a matter of hours instead of weeks. But I would say we're still far from the point where you hand a robot a new task and it just figures it out. Right now adaptation is something an engineer does, not something the robot does, and closing that gap is really the core research question for the next few years.

r001.rationale: The response says adapting to new tasks is difficult, but it never compares that challenge with adapting to a new robot.

r002.rationale: It identifies human time as the main cost of adaptation and describes progress as reducing the effort to add a task from weeks to hours.

astra-6.text:
I think the challenge is that a task that looks very similar to us can be quite different for a robot. You might train a policy to walk on one kind of terrain, and then a change in friction or the height of an obstacle can require different behavior. So we want the robot to learn something more general than a solution to one very specific situation.

One approach is to expose it to a wide range of conditions during training, especially in simulation, where we can vary those conditions relatively cheaply. But that raises another question: is the robot actually able to adapt, or have we just trained it on enough variations that the new task happens to be covered? Getting robots to reuse what they have learned and acquire a new skill with very little additional experience is still a difficult problem.

r001.rationale: It describes adapting to new tasks as difficult but does not compare that difficulty with adapting to a new robot.

r002.rationale: It discusses training variation and additional experience, but does not identify human effort as a key progress metric.

sol-6.1.text: I think the key challenge is getting robots to generalize. You can train a policy to do one task very well, but if you change the environment or ask it to do something slightly different, you may have to train it again. For a robot to be useful, it needs to adapt without requiring a huge amount of data and engineering for every new task. And it has to do that reliably, because mistakes in the physical world have consequences. So there’s a balance between learning skills that transfer across tasks and being able to learn the specifics of a new task quickly.
